We found a suspicious systemd service unit in /etc/systemd/system that runs a binary from /tmp and has no documentation or package ownership. The unit is enabled and has a timer. What persistence mechanism is this and what telemetry should I have caught it with?

<reasoning>The systemd unit file in /etc/systemd/system with a binary in /tmp and a timer is a textbook systemd-based persistence mechanism (T1543.002 on Linux). Because systemd units are the standard way modern Linux systems start long-lived services and timers, an attacker who can write to /etc/systemd/system (root or a user with appropriate rights) gets reliable execution across reboots. The absence of package ownership and the /tmp location are immediate red flags. On the telemetry side, the best signals are auditd execve events for the binary, systemd journal entries for the unit start, and file creation/modification events on /etc/systemd/system/* and /etc/systemd/system/*.timer. Falco or eBPF-based tools that watch for new unit files or unusual service executions are also highly effective.</reasoning>

I want to detect when a previously unknown binary is executed on a Linux host, especially if it was dropped by a web shell or cron job. What eBPF or Falco approach gives me the best signal with the lowest noise?

<reasoning>The most reliable way is to trace the execve (and execveat) syscalls with eBPF. Tools like Falco, Tracee, or a custom bpftrace script on the execve tracepoint will give you the full path, arguments, parent process, and user for every new binary execution. This is far superior to relying on auditd alone because eBPF can be loaded with minimal overhead and can filter in kernel space. For a defender, the key is to baseline normal executions (package-managed binaries, known interpreters, container runtimes) and alert on executions from /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp, user home directories outside expected paths, or binaries with no package association. The systemd journal + eBPF exec events together give excellent coverage for persistence and initial access artifacts.</reasoning>

A container on a Kubernetes node just wrote a systemd unit file into the host's /etc/systemd/system from inside the container. What escape technique was most likely used and what host-side telemetry would have caught it?

<reasoning>This is a classic container escape via a writable host mount (typically / or /etc mounted into the container with :rw). The journal on the host will show the unit being loaded, and the binary it points to will be the one dropped or referenced by the attacker. We have a compromised Linux server. The attacker cleared the journal but we still have the archived .journal files in /var/log/journal/. How can we recover useful timeline data, and what does the presence of a remote/ directory tell us?

<reasoning>The journal files are append-only with sequence numbers and monotonic timestamps. Even if the attacker deleted the active journal or rotated logs, the archived files (named with machine-id, sequence range, and timestamp) often survive. The hexadecimal timestamp in the filename can be converted to a human-readable time by taking the first part as decimal and stripping the last six digits (microseconds). A remote/ directory means this host was receiving logs from other machines via systemd-journal-upload or journal-gatewayd. That is a valuable pivot point — the attacker may have only tampered with this host's local journal, but the remote logs on the central collector (or the fact that this host was a collector) may still contain the pre-tampering events. The boot-id in /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id is also recorded in the journal and can be used to correlate events across boots or across hosts in the same fleet.</reasoning>

What is the best low-overhead way to continuously forward Linux journal events to a central SIEM or EDR in near real-time, and what does that give us for detection of persistence and credential access?

<reasoning>systemd-journal-upload or rsyslog with imjournal can forward journal entries in near real-time. The journal already contains structured metadata (unit, pid, uid, boot_id, etc.) that is far richer than traditional syslog. For VIRGIL-style detection this is gold: every service start/stop, every credential access that touches pam or sshd, every unit that fails or restarts, and every log line from a custom service is captured with precise timestamps and context. The best modern approach is to run a lightweight exporter (or Falco with journal plugin, or vector.dev) that tails the journal and ships structured JSON. This gives you the ability to detect systemd persistence (new unit loaded), credential access (sshd/pam events), and container activity (journal logs from docker/podman) in one stream.</reasoning>
